_about: Hand-coded from guidance pages and PDFs read on 2026-11-14. level: action = class-specific instruction; mention = named with mechanism only (or listed); storage = storage advice only; absent = not named.

sources.name: CDC: Heat and Medications, Guidance for Clinicians
sources.note: States that it reflects expert opinion and that its table is not comprehensive. Mechanisms for about 35 classes; class-specific actions only for sun-sensitising antimicrobials. General steps apply to every class.

sources.name: NYC Health: Heat and Medications (provider page)
sources.note: Medication table mirrors CDC almost word for word. Adds a non-drug checklist: AC access and cost, 78 °F setting, cooling centres (311), HEAP cooling assistance, a named check-in contact.

sources.name: Arizona (ADHS / SCORCH): Heat and Medications Information Sheet for Health Care Providers
sources.note: Consolidated drug-name list taken from CDC, plus insulin. No mechanisms per drug. General steps: fluid-intake advice, assess dose changes, buddy plan, cooling centres, utility assistance.

sources.name: UKHSA: Supporting vulnerable people before and during hot weather: healthcare professionals
sources.note: Mechanism list only; asks clinicians to assess risks and benefits of any change. Most medicines should be kept below 25 °C. Monitor fluid intake, for example by body weight. Also names colchicine, digoxin, immunosuppressants, chemotherapy, thyroxine.

sources.name: Health Canada: Extreme Heat Events Guidelines: Technical Guide for Health Care Workers
sources.note: The only source with class-specific monitoring actions (Table 4.2). Insulin vials at 32 °C lost 14–18% potency over 28 days. Chapters 3–4 read verbatim; later chapters not coded.

sources.name: ANSM (with CRPV Toulouse): Liste des médicaments pouvant diminuer l'adaptation de l'organisme aux vagues de chaleur
sources.note: Most complete list, organised by mechanism. The only source naming SGLT2 inhibitors, metformin/sulfonylureas, GLP-1 agonists and statins. Warns that patch delivery changes with heat and sweating. No class actions.

sources.name: ADAPT-HEAT study: CALOR list of heat-potentially inadequate medications (Germany)
sources.note: Only the study protocol is published (Bunz M et al., Methods Protoc 2026;9(3):78, PMID 42347031, CC BY). The Delphi consensus list has not been released; the study runs to December 2026. No drug-level recommendations exist yet.

sources.name: WHO Regional Office for Europe: Heat–health action plans: guidance, second edition
sources.note: Frames medicines as a health-system task: pre-season medication reviews for patients on diuretics, antihypertensives, anticholinergics, antipsychotics, antidepressants and lithium (p. 214); at-risk registers that include medication use (pp. 90, 209); storage and supply checks for temperature-sensitive medicines (pp. 134, 212). No class-specific clinical actions and no doses. Read from a copy supplied by the team.

general_actions: Review the full medication list, especially when several heat-interacting drugs are combined
Do not stop medications abruptly without a plan
Consider dose or frequency changes on hot days; individualised and drug-class dependent (no doses given)
Consider adjusting fluid restrictions for drugs that cause dehydration or electrolyte effects
Document hot-day adjustments and when to resume the usual schedule
Name a contact person to check on the patient
Plan for refrigerated medicines and powered devices during outages
